name: Octocrylene
lead: Octocrylene is an organic ultraviolet filter and photostabilizer used in sunscreens and other cosmetics. It is an ester (C24H27NO2) that absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA light, and it is commonly added to stabilize avobenzone.[1][2]

It has been the subject of scrutiny on three fronts: systemic absorption seen in US clinical trials, slow degradation into benzophenone in stored products, and environmental effects reported in laboratory studies of corals and other marine organisms.[1][3][4]
Several jurisdictions that restrict reef-toxic sunscreen ingredients, such as Palau and the US Virgin Islands, have included it in their restrictions.[1]

paras: Octocrylene is made by Knoevenagel condensation of 2-ethylhexyl cyanoacetate with benzophenone.[1] Its conjugated acrylate portion absorbs light in the UVB and short UVA range, while its ethylhexyl chain adds emollient, water-resistant properties.[1] Because it stays largely unchanged under irradiation, it is used to stabilize less photostable filters such as avobenzone.[2]

Wikipedia notes that octocrylene can penetrate skin, is excreted in urine as metabolites, and can act as a photosensitizer in light.[1] The two JAMA randomized trials of sunscreen under maximal-use conditions included octocrylene among the actives detected in plasma, above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold for further toxicology assessment; the trials did not assess clinical harm.[5][6]

Octocrylene can degrade into benzophenone through a slow retro-aldol reaction, and Wikipedia reports that benzophenone was found in every commercial cosmetic tested that contained octocrylene.[1] Octocrylene and other UV filters have also been measured in human breast milk in a cohort of mother-child pairs.[7]

Surveys in Switzerland, Japan and Norway detected octocrylene and other UV filters in lakes, rivers, sediment, wastewater and fish.[8][9][10][11][12] A 2019 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology examined environmental effects of oxybenzone and other sunscreen ingredients. In corals, Wikipedia reports that octocrylene accumulates as fatty acid conjugates and probably triggers mitochondrial dysfunction.[1]

Palau's 2018 Responsible Tourism Education Act restricted octocrylene along with other reef-toxic filters, and the US Virgin Islands prohibits octocrylene sunscreens and requires non-nano mineral products.[1] Grokipedia states that the FDA and EU's SCCS permit it up to 10 percent.[2]

Human data are mainly pharmacokinetic. The 2019 and 2020 JAMA randomized clinical trials measured plasma concentrations of octocrylene after sunscreen application and found it above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold.[5][6] They did not evaluate dermatologic outcomes or harm.

card.summary: A photostable UVB filter used mainly to keep avobenzone from breaking down, with open questions over absorption, benzophenone formation and reef effects.
card.note: Systemically absorbed in trials; can degrade into benzophenone; restricted in Palau and the US Virgin Islands.

quick.overview:
Octocrylene is a UVB-absorbing sunscreen ingredient that also stabilizes avobenzone. It is common in chemical sunscreens and in cosmetics with SPF.

It has drawn attention for being absorbed into the body, for slowly forming benzophenone in products, and for environmental concerns.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs UVB and short-wave UVA light and is itself largely photostable, so it helps keep other filters from degrading.
quick.risks: Clinical trials detected it in plasma above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold, with unknown clinical significance. Some places restrict it for reef-protection reasons.
